Literal Interpretation

The Opening Declaration

The first chapter of Genesis presents the foundational account of God's creative work, establishing the origin of all visible and invisible reality. The opening words, "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth" (Gen 1:1), assert three essential truths: that creation had a beginning in time, that God alone is the Creator, and that all things owe their existence entirely to His sovereign will.

St. Basil the Great, in his celebrated Hexaemeron, emphasizes the importance of this declaration against pagan philosophy:

"It is right that any one beginning to narrate the formation of the world should begin with the good order which reigns in visible things. I am about to speak of the creation of heaven and earth, which was not spontaneous, as some have imagined, but drew its origin from God."

St. Basil the Great, Hexaemeron, Homily I

The Hebrew word bara (to create) is used exclusively of divine action in Scripture, signifying creation ex nihilo—from nothing. This stands in stark contrast to ancient Near Eastern cosmogonies, which typically portrayed the gods fashioning the world from pre-existent matter or from the bodies of defeated deities.

The Six Days of Creation

The narrative proceeds through six days of creative activity, each introduced by the divine command "Let there be" (fiat). St. Augustine, in his De Genesi ad Litteram, wrestled extensively with the nature of these "days," noting their unique character:

"It is indeed an arduous and extremely difficult task for us to get through to what the writer meant with these six days, however concentrated our attention and lively our minds."

St. Augustine, De Genesi ad Litteram

Augustine affirms that these days "are not at all like" ordinary twenty-four-hour days, "but very, very different." His concern was not to diminish the historical reality of creation, but to understand properly what the sacred author intended to convey.

The Structure of the Days

The six days exhibit a careful literary structure, with the first three days establishing realms or domains, and the final three days populating those domains with their respective inhabitants:

  • Day 1: Light separated from darkness (realm of light/darkness)
  • Day 2: Firmament separates waters above from waters below (realm of sky/sea)
  • Day 3: Dry land appears; vegetation springs forth (realm of land)
  • Day 4: Sun, moon, and stars placed in the firmament (rulers of light/darkness)
  • Day 5: Sea creatures and birds created (inhabitants of sky/sea)
  • Day 6: Land animals and man created (inhabitants of land)

Creation by Divine Word

Throughout the chapter, creation occurs by the power of God's Word. St. John Chrysostom, in his Homilies on Genesis, draws attention to the manner in which the Holy Spirit reveals the order of created things:

"The Holy Spirit, in his foreknowledge of future events, teaches the order of created things—what was created first and what second—and that from the earth, in compliance with the Lord's word, the earth produced plants without depending on the sun for assistance."

St. John Chrysostom, Homilies on Genesis

This observation—that vegetation was created on the third day before the sun on the fourth—demonstrates the absolute sovereignty of God over nature. The plants did not need the sun to exist because God's Word alone sustains all things.

The Goodness of Creation

Seven times in this chapter we read that God saw His work and declared it "good" (tov), with the final assessment being "very good" (tov meod) after the creation of man. St. Basil addresses the origin of evil in light of this:

"It is equally impious to say that evil has its origin from God; because the contrary cannot proceed from its contrary. Life does not engender death; darkness is not the origin of light; sickness is not the maker of health... Evil is not a living animated essence; it is the condition of the soul opposed to virtue, developed in the careless on account of their falling away from good."

St. Basil the Great, Hexaemeron

The Creation of Man

The climax of the creation narrative is the formation of man on the sixth day. Unlike the other creatures, man is created after a divine deliberation: "Let us make man in our image, after our likeness" (Gen 1:26). St. Ambrose of Milan reflects on the exceptional dignity of man:

"Man for St. Ambrose is an exceptional creature; he is God's masterpiece, the synthesis and end of all creation. At the end of the six days, God creates a creature that encompasses both matter and spirit in a profound balance."

Summary of St. Ambrose, Hexaemeron

The plural "Let us make" has been understood by the Church Fathers as an intimation of the Holy Trinity—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—deliberating together in the creation of man. This interpretation finds support in the Trinitarian reading of the entire chapter, where the Father creates, the Word (Logos) speaks, and the Spirit hovers over the waters.

Male and Female

"Male and female he created them" (Gen 1:27). The sexual differentiation of humanity is part of the original divine plan, ordered toward fruitfulness and the filling of the earth. Both man and woman share equally in the imago Dei.

The Dominion Mandate

Man is given dominion over the fish of the sea, the birds of the air, and every living thing that moves upon the earth (Gen 1:28). This is not a license for exploitation but a vocation of stewardship, exercised in imitation of God's own providential care for His creation.

Allegorical Interpretation

Christ the Eternal Word

The opening words of Genesis, "In the beginning" (Bereshit), find their fullest meaning in the prologue to St. John's Gospel: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God" (Jn 1:1). The Church Fathers consistently interpreted Genesis 1 in light of Christ, the Eternal Logos through whom all things were made.

St. Augustine defends this time-honored tradition of patristic exegesis:

"'In the beginning God made heaven and earth' means that by his Word coeternal with himself God made the intelligible and sensible worlds."

St. Augustine, De Genesi ad Litteram

Augustine argues that those who take "In the beginning" to invoke merely the concept of "time" miss the deeper meaning. His preferred interpretation—"In the Word, God created the heaven and earth"—reveals that Christ was present and active at creation. The phrase Bereshit can be rendered "In the Principle," and Christ is the Arche, the Principle and Foundation of all things.

The Trinity in Genesis 1

The presence of the Holy Trinity is discernible from the first verses of Scripture. The Father is the Creator who speaks; the Word (Logos) is the one through whom all things are made; and the Spirit of God (Ruach Elohim) hovers over the face of the waters (Gen 1:2). Augustine's reading was thoroughly Trinitarian:

"Jesus as the Word of God, and the Holy Spirit brooding over the waters, were seen in the account of creation, along with the Father."

Summary of St. Augustine's Trinitarian interpretation

Light as Figure of Christ

"And God said: Let there be light. And there was light" (Gen 1:3). The first created thing is light, and Christ declares Himself to be "the light of the world" (Jn 8:12). The separation of light from darkness on the first day prefigures the coming of Christ, who separates truth from error, holiness from sin, the children of light from the children of darkness.

St. Basil the Great concludes his homily on the first day with a prayer that connects the physical light to Christ:

"May the Father of the true light, Who has adorned day with celestial light, Who has made the fire to shine which illuminates us during the night, Who reserves for us in the peace of a future age a spiritual and everlasting light, enlighten your hearts in the knowledge of truth... Thus shall you shine as the sun in the midst of the glory of the saints."

St. Basil the Great, Hexaemeron, Homily II

The Six Days and the Passion

The Fathers saw a profound typological connection between the six days of creation and the work of redemption. On the sixth day, God crowned His creative work with the formation of Adam. It is no accident that Christ, the New Adam, accomplished His redemptive work on Friday, the sixth day of the week. As the first Adam was formed from the earth on the sixth day, so the New Adam was lifted up on the Cross on the sixth day to restore what Adam had lost.

Eve and the Church

The creation of woman from the side of Adam (Gen 2:21-22, which expands on the sixth day's work mentioned in 1:27) is a type of the Church's birth from the pierced side of Christ on the Cross. When the centurion pierced Christ's sacred side, there flowed blood and water—the sacraments of the Eucharist and Baptism—by which the Church, the Bride of Christ, is constituted.

"The Church is the spouse of Christ; she is the new Eve created from the pierced side of the New Adam. The mysterious significance of Eve being created from Adam's side can only be grasped through the Passion of Christ."

Traditional patristic interpretation

The Waters and Baptism

The waters that appear throughout Genesis 1—over which the Spirit hovers, which are separated by the firmament, which are gathered into seas—prefigure the waters of Baptism. Just as the Spirit moved over the primordial waters to bring forth life, so the Spirit descends upon the baptismal waters to bring forth new life in Christ. The emergence of dry land from the waters on the third day anticipates both the crossing of the Red Sea and the resurrection of Christ on the third day.

The Firmament and the Cross

The firmament (raqia) that divides the waters above from the waters below has been understood as a figure of the Cross, which stands between heaven and earth, uniting what was divided by sin. Through the Cross, access to the "waters above"—the heavenly realm—is restored to mankind.

Vegetation and the Church

The creation of vegetation on the third day, yielding seed according to its kind, prefigures the Church, which brings forth spiritual fruit through the preaching of the Gospel. The seed that falls into the ground and dies to bring forth much fruit is Christ Himself, and the abundant harvest is the communion of saints.

St. Basil notes that the rose was originally without thorns:

"But then the rose was without thorns; since then the thorn has been added to its beauty, to make us feel that sorrow is very near to pleasure, and to remind us of our sin, which condemned the earth to produce thorns and caltrops."

St. Basil the Great, Hexaemeron, Homily V

The thorns that now accompany the rose point forward to the crown of thorns placed upon Christ's head—the curse of sin transformed into a crown of glory.

Man as Image of Christ

Man, created in the image and likeness of God (Gen 1:26-27), is ultimately an image of Christ, who is Himself "the image of the invisible God" (Col 1:15). The imago Dei in man is fully realized and restored in Christ. Through union with Christ in baptism, believers are conformed to the One who is the perfect image of the Father.

Moral (Tropological) Interpretation

The Call to Co-Creation

Genesis 1 is not merely an account of what God did "in the beginning" but a revelation of how the faithful are called to live. The creative activity of God establishes the pattern for human action: purposeful, ordered, good, and fruitful. As God worked and then rested, so man is called to meaningful labor and holy rest.

Order Against Chaos

"And the earth was void and empty, and darkness was upon the face of the deep" (Gen 1:2). Before God's creative word, there was tohu wa-bohu—formlessness and void. God's work throughout the six days is to bring order out of chaos, form out of formlessness, light out of darkness. This is the moral pattern for the Christian life: by God's grace, we are called to bring order to our disordered passions, form to our formless lives, and the light of virtue to the darkness of vice.

The Power of the Word

God creates by speaking: "Let there be light." The moral lesson is profound—words have creative power. The Christian is called to use speech for building up, not tearing down; for blessing, not cursing; for truth, not falsehood. As God's Word brings life and goodness into being, our words should bring forth the fruits of charity and peace.

Separation and Discernment

A recurring theme in Genesis 1 is separation: light from darkness, waters above from waters below, day from night, sea from dry land. God's creative work involves making distinctions. The moral application is the virtue of discernment—the ability to distinguish good from evil, truth from error, the holy from the profane. The faithful Christian must cultivate this capacity for judgment, not in a spirit of condemnation, but in pursuit of holiness.

St. Basil reflects on the separation of light and darkness:

"God does not say the darkness was good, or evil for that matter. Now, darkness is not evil but is an allegory for evil. It is a privation of light, which God allows but does not create... God's work is perfectly good and visible without even a hint of darkness."

Summary of St. Basil's teaching

The Imago Dei and Human Dignity

The creation of man in the image and likeness of God (Gen 1:26-27) is the foundation of all Christian ethics. Every human person, regardless of age, ability, or circumstance, bears the divine image and possesses inviolable dignity. This truth has profound moral implications:

  • Respect for Life: Because every person is made in God's image, human life is sacred from conception to natural death.
  • Love of Neighbor: To love God requires loving those who bear His image. As the moral implications of the imago Dei make clear, "if humans are to love God, then humans must love other humans whom God has created, as each is an expression of God."
  • Self-Respect: The Christian must also recognize his or her own dignity as an image-bearer, avoiding all that degrades or defiles the human person.

St. Augustine understood the image of God as the power of reason and understanding:

"When man fell, the image of God was corrupted. The participation of the soul in God was lost, but God restores this loss of participation through redemption."

Summary of St. Augustine's teaching on the imago Dei

Dominion as Stewardship

"Fill the earth and subdue it, and rule over the fishes of the sea, and the fowls of the air, and all living creatures that move upon the earth" (Gen 1:28). The dominion given to man is not a license for exploitation but a vocation of stewardship. Man is called to exercise authority over creation in imitation of God's own providential care—nurturing, protecting, and ordering creation toward its proper ends. The abuse of nature is a moral failing, a betrayal of the trust God has placed in humanity.

Fruitfulness and Generosity

"Be fruitful and multiply" (Gen 1:28). The first blessing given to man is that of fruitfulness. Beyond its application to marriage and family, this command calls all Christians to spiritual fruitfulness—to bear the fruits of the Spirit, to multiply disciples, to be generous with the gifts God has given. A life closed in on itself, refusing to give and share, contradicts the creative abundance revealed in Genesis 1.

The Sanctification of Time

The structure of the six days followed by rest establishes a pattern for the sanctification of time. Work is good and holy when ordered toward God and neighbor. But work is not ultimate—it must yield to rest, worship, and contemplation. The refusal to rest, the idolization of productivity, is a spiritual disorder that denies God's lordship over time.

Humility Before the Creator

St. Basil warns against intellectual pride in matters of creation:

"The philosophers of Greece have made much ado to explain nature, and not one of their systems has remained firm and unshaken, each being overturned by its successor. It is vain to refute them; they are sufficient in themselves to destroy one another."

St. Basil the Great, Hexaemeron, Homily I

The proper response to Genesis 1 is wonder and humility, not the presumption that we can fully comprehend or explain God's creative work. As St. Gregory of Nazianzus wrote of Basil's homilies: "Whenever I take his Hexaemeron in hand and quote its words, I am brought face to face with my Creator: I begin to understand the method of creation: I feel more awe than ever I did before, when I only looked at God's work with my eyes."

Living in the Light

The moral life is a movement from darkness to light. Those who walk in the light of Christ practice the virtues, flee from sin, and grow in holiness. As the physical light was the first of God's creative works, so the light of grace must be the first thing we seek each day, illuminating all our thoughts, words, and deeds.

Anagogical Interpretation

Creation and the New Creation

The anagogical sense of Scripture interprets earthly realities as signs pointing to eternal glory. Genesis 1, which narrates the first creation, finds its ultimate fulfillment in the new creation promised in Christ. As St. John beholds in his vision: "And I saw a new heaven and a new earth. For the first heaven and the first earth was gone" (Rev 21:1). The original creation, though marred by sin, is not destined for annihilation but for transformation and glorification.

The Eighth Day

The seven days of creation culminate in the Sabbath rest, but Christian tradition speaks of an "eighth day"—the day of resurrection, the day that transcends the weekly cycle and inaugurates eternity. Christ rose on the first day of the week, which is also the eighth day, the day beyond the Sabbath. This eighth day is the eternal day of the new creation, when time itself will be taken up into the timelessness of God.

The Sabbath Rest and Eternal Life

The seventh day, on which God rested from His work, is a type of the eternal rest that awaits the faithful in heaven. The Letter to the Hebrews develops this theme extensively: "There remaineth therefore a day of rest for the people of God" (Heb 4:9). The earthly Sabbath is a foretaste and pledge of that heavenly rest where all labor, sorrow, and struggle will cease.

"The Sabbath points backward to the rest of creation lost in the fall and forward to the heavenly rest which belongs to those who believe in Christ."

Traditional theological interpretation

This eschatological rest is not mere inactivity but the fullness of beatitude—the perfect enjoyment of God in the communion of saints. As one theologian expressed it: "The Sabbath rest is typological of the future rest of all believers in the new heavens and new earth... in which the saints, happy in souls and body, will rest in God from the sins, calamities, and miseries of this life."

Paradise Restored

The garden planted by God, with its abundance of fruit-bearing trees (Gen 1:29), anticipates the heavenly paradise. In the Book of Revelation, the tree of life, lost to humanity after the fall, stands in the midst of the heavenly city, and its leaves are "for the healing of the nations" (Rev 22:2). What was closed in Genesis will be opened in glory; what was lost through sin will be restored through grace, superabundantly.

The Communion of Heaven and Earth

"In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth" (Gen 1:1). Heaven and earth, though distinct, are created together in the beginning and will be united fully in the end. The Lord's Prayer teaches us to pray that God's will be done "on earth as it is in heaven"—a petition that looks forward to the final consummation when the heavenly and earthly realms will be perfectly harmonized in Christ.

"The twinning of heaven and earth is amplified in the eschatological teaching, where Jesus declares that 'heaven and earth' will pass away (Mark 13:31), and both Peter and John the visionary catch a glimpse of 'new heavens and new earth.'"

St Andrews Encyclopaedia of Theology, "New Creation"

Light Eternal

The creation of light on the first day prefigures the eternal light of heaven, where "they shall not need the light of the lamp, nor the light of the sun, because the Lord God shall enlighten them" (Rev 22:5). In the new creation, there will be no alternation of day and night, no mixture of light and darkness, but the unchanging radiance of God's glory illuminating all things.

St. Basil the Great prays for this eternal light:

"May the Father of the true light, Who reserves for us in the peace of a future age a spiritual and everlasting light, enlighten your hearts in the knowledge of truth... Thus shall you shine as the sun in the midst of the glory of the saints."

St. Basil the Great, Hexaemeron

The Glorified Image

Man, created in the image and likeness of God, is destined for glorification. The imago Dei, wounded by original sin, is restored in baptism and will be perfected in the resurrection of the body. "We know that when he shall appear, we shall be like to him: because we shall see him as he is" (1 Jn 3:2). The beatific vision—seeing God face to face—is the ultimate fulfillment of what it means to be made in God's image.

The Cosmic Liturgy

The orderly progression of the six days, with each element praising God by fulfilling its created purpose, anticipates the eternal liturgy of heaven. The sun, moon, and stars; the sea creatures and birds; the beasts of the field—all creation joins in the cosmic hymn of praise. In heaven, this worship reaches its perfection as the whole creation, led by the redeemed, offers unending glory to the Creator.

The New Adam and the New Eve

The creation of Adam and Eve on the sixth day points toward Christ and Mary, the New Adam and New Eve, and ultimately toward the marriage of the Lamb and His Bride, the Church. The union of man and woman in paradise is a type of the eternal union between Christ and His people in the heavenly Jerusalem, where the wedding feast of the Lamb will be celebrated forever.

Already and Not Yet

The new creation is both present and future. Through baptism and life in Christ, believers already participate in the new creation: "If then any be in Christ a new creature, the old things are passed away. Behold all things are made new" (2 Cor 5:17). Yet the fullness of the new creation awaits the second coming of Christ, when He will make all things new and God will be "all in all."

"Because the turning point of the human story is the incarnation, the New Testament does not always envisage the new creation as future but as something inaugurated. Christ has lived the righteous life intended for Adam and Eve, has conquered death, been raised, and glorified, and the Holy Spirit has been given to the faithful."

St Andrews Encyclopaedia of Theology, "New Creation"

The Ultimate Sabbath

The seventh day of rest, with which the creation narrative concludes, is left mysteriously open-ended—Scripture does not say "and there was evening and morning, the seventh day." The Sabbath remains unfulfilled, awaiting its consummation in the eternal rest of heaven. Christ invites all who labor and are burdened to find rest in Him, and this rest, begun in grace, will be perfected in glory. The whole of human history moves toward that ultimate Sabbath when the work of redemption will be complete and God's people will enter into the joy of their Lord forever.
